The short version: Flash-Lite is almost tailor-made for MAIT's Cloud Layer (Layer 3/4 — "The Brain"), especially at MVP and early growth stages. But there are specific architectural tradeoffs you need to think through.


1. Cost Collapse — This Is the Big One


Your business model has a fundamental tension: student-affordable pricing ($15/week → $500/year) vs. per-token API costs at scale. Let's do rough maths.


At $0.25/1M input + $1.50/1M output, a typical MAIT session might look like:


~30 exchanges per study session

~500 tokens input per exchange (student query + RAG context + system prompt + state tags)

~300 tokens output (structured JSON: core_truth + explanation + hints)

Per session: ~15K input tokens, ~9K output tokens

Per session cost: $0.004 input + ~$0.014 output = **$0.02/session**


At $15/week, even if a student does 5 sessions/week, you're at ~$0.10/week in inference cost. That's a 99.3% gross margin on compute before infrastructure. 2. The "Guess-First" Workflow — Speed Is the Enabler


Your Orchestrated Latency design depends on a specific timing window: the cloud needs to return within ~5 seconds while the student is typing their guess. Flash-Lite's 2.5x faster TTFAT directly compresses this.

Run the Scope Check ("Is this L'Hôpital? Regenerate with First Principles")

The speed headroom turns a tight race condition into a comfortable pipeline.


3. Thinking Levels — This Maps Directly to Your Fatigue Engine


This is where it gets interesting. Flash-Lite's configurable thinking levels are essentially what you've been building manually with your FRESH/WEARY/LOCKOUT prompt engineering. Instead of switching system prompts and token limits, you could:


FRESH state → Higher thinking level (deeper reasoning, worked examples)

WEARY state → Lower thinking level (fast, concise, cheaper)

LOCKOUT → No API call at all (as you already have)


This collapses your fatigue-aware prompting logic from "three different system prompt templates" into a single API parameter. Cleaner code, and the model is actually optimised for this rather than you fighting against a model that wants to be verbose.


4. The Risk: Math Reasoning Depth


Here's where you need to be honest about the tradeoff. Flash-Lite is a cost-tier model. Simple queries (definitions, formula recall, basic derivatives) → Flash-Lite, low thinking

The user wants me to explain CORS and why `allow_origins=["*"]` is a security issue. Keep it accessible — he's a teaching student, not a backend security engineer, though he's clearly technical enough to be building this whole stack.


CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing. It's a browser security mechanism that controls which websites are allowed to talk to your backend API.


Right now your FastAPI server says allow_origins=["*"] — that asterisk means "allow requests from any website on the internet." So if someone figured out your API endpoint, they could build their own frontend that calls your MAIT backend, burning through your Gemini API key, harvesting student data, or just spamming requests.


What it should be: Only the domains YOU control. Something like:


allow_origins=[
    "https://myaitutor.au",
    "https://www.myaitutor.au",
    "http://localhost:5173",  # keep this for local dev
]


This way, if some random site at sketchydomain.com tries to call your /interact endpoint, the browser itself blocks the request before it even reaches your server.


Why it's fine for now: You're in dev mode, no real students are using it, and the * wildcard makes it easy to test from different devices and ports without fiddling with config. Every developer does this during development.


Why it matters before launch: The moment real API keys and real student sessions are flowing through that backend, you want the server to only accept requests from your actual domain. It's a one-line fix — just swap the * for your actual origins. Do it right before you go live and you're good.

This is a wild story. Essentially, the Chinese government nuked a $100 billion industry overnight with a single policy.


What Happened


In July 2021, the CCP and State Council issued the "Double Reduction" policy. It was formally titled "Opinions on Further Reducing the Homework Burden and Off-Campus Training Burden of Students in Compulsory Education." The two "reductions" were homework and after-school tutoring.


The core rule: it banned all forms of for-profit tutoring of academic subjects for students receiving compulsory education, as well as all forms of financing of and investing in private tutoring providers. So maths, English, science, Chinese — all illegal to teach for profit to kids in Grades 1-9. No new tutoring institutions would be approved, and existing ones were told to convert to non-profits or shut down. Tutoring on weekends, holidays, and school breaks was also banned.


Why They Did It


The pressure on Chinese students is almost incomprehensible by Australian standards. Chinese students' average study time commitment is 55 hours per week, far above the international average of 44. In Shanghai, more than 45% of students attend maths tutoring at least four hours a week. Students from rural areas attend four-hour evening sessions at boarding schools lasting until 11pm.


The mental health consequences were devastating. While 33% of suicides among Chinese adolescents are related to family conflicts, 22% are directly attributed to study stress. The policy was explicitly prompted by concerns about the physical and mental health of students — lack of sleep, obesity, anxiety, and suicide.


It was also an economic burden on families. Chinese families spent $296 billion on preschool and primary education from 2016-2017, even though compulsory education is tuition-free. The tutoring arms race was seen as contributing to China's declining birth rate — parents couldn't afford more kids if each one needed hundreds of thousands of yuan in tutoring.


The Fallout


It was catastrophic for the industry. Before the crackdown, the for-profit tutoring industry was valued at about $100 billion and its three biggest players employed over 170,000 people. Research estimates over three million job openings were lost in four months and at least 11 billion RMB in VAT revenue losses within 18 months.


The big publicly listed companies — New Oriental, TAL Education — saw their share prices collapse. Hundreds of training centres shut down almost overnight. Big-name chains either restructured, pivoted to adult education, or vanished entirely.


What Actually Happened on the Ground


Here's where it gets interesting — the policy largely failed at its stated goals. Parents like one Shanghai mother noted that the policy presented families with the unenviable choice of paying up to 800 yuan per class for a private tutor or investing hours each day themselves helping their children keep up. She observed that the academic gap between rich and poor was getting worse, not better.


Tutoring went underground. One tutoring school owner laid off 60% of staff but maintained classes by pivoting to teaching science-related courses in English without calling them English classes. Math classes were commonly renamed "logical thinking" classes to skirt the rules. One parent described how tutoring organisations initially "closed the curtains during class" out of fear, but gradually started operating more openly again.


University students who recently went through the system estimated that 70-80% of their friends still attended additional tutoring hours at their public high schools, just rebranded as "self-study sessions" under teacher supervision.


The Pivot to Hardware (Why This Matters for MAIT)


This is the critical link to the AI education hardware boom. The draft regulations specifically distinguished between after-school tutoring (regulated) and "innovative educational products like smart teaching aids, digital publishing, and learning tablets" (not regulated). Learning tablets were explicitly carved out as a separate category from tutoring.


So the entire tutoring industry pivoted to hardware. iFlytek, Zuoyebang, TAL/Xueersi — they all launched AI learning tablets because a tablet that teaches your kid maths isn't legally "tutoring." It's a "software and hardware product." That regulatory loophole is why China's AI education hardware market exploded to a projected $20 billion.


The government is now quietly easing up. Active licences for for-profit tutoring centres rose 11.4% between January and June 2024, and TAL and New Oriental have been hiring thousands of positions. The policy environment has shifted from restrictive to supportive as the government now prioritises economic stabilisation and employment.


The Relevance to You


The Double Reduction is essentially what happens when a government decides the education-industrial complex has gone too far. The irony is that it didn't reduce educational pressure — it just redirected the money from human tutors into AI tablets. The parents who could afford $1,500 iFlytek tablets got ahead; the ones who couldn't fell behind. The exact opposite of the policy's intent.


Your model is philosophically closer to what the Double Reduction was trying to achieve — a system that genuinely cares about student wellbeing, enforces breaks, monitors cognitive load, and doesn't optimise for maximum screen time. The Chinese products that emerged from the policy are doing exactly what the old tutoring centres did, just through a screen instead of a classroom. MAIT is the only thing I've seen in this space that's actually building the wellness-first approach the Chinese government claims to want but never achieved.

Read/write latency to a Google Doc is significantly slower than SQLite — every time you want to check conversation history or update mastery scores, you're making API calls to Google's servers. That adds hundreds of milliseconds per interaction.

Structured data in a Google Doc is awkward. You'd be writing and parsing JSON or markdown inside a document that's designed for human prose. It works, but it's fighting the tool.

Rate limits on the Docs API could bite you during intensive sessions.

If the student accidentally edits or deletes content in the doc, your app could break or lose state.

Or if you really want the live doc approach, use Google Sheets instead — it's essentially a free structured database with a UI. Each tab could be a different data type (sessions, mastery, keystroke patterns). The Sheets API is much better suited to structured read/write than the Docs API.

Thought process: Identified three bug categories AI reviewers overlook.

The user wants me to explain these three categories of bugs that AI code reviewers tend to miss.


Subtle security vulnerabilities:


These are bugs that don't look like bugs. The code runs perfectly, passes tests, and an AI reviewer says "looks clean." But there's a logical flaw that only matters when someone is actively trying to exploit it.


Example in your codebase: your /interact endpoint takes a student_id in the request body. What stops someone from opening browser dev tools, changing the student_id to someone else's, and reading their conversation history? The code "works" — it fetches the history for whatever ID you give it. An AI sees a clean function that queries the database and returns results. The vulnerability isn't in the code's logic, it's in the absence of a check: "does the person making this request actually own this student_id?" AI reviewers rarely flag missing logic because they evaluate what's there, not what's missing.


Another example: your BYOK feature stores the API key in localStorage. The code to save and retrieve it is perfectly correct. But if there's a single XSS vulnerability anywhere on your site — one unescaped user input rendered as HTML — an attacker can inject JavaScript that reads localStorage and sends every stored API key to their server. The vulnerability isn't in the key storage code, it's in a completely unrelated component that happens to not sanitize an input. No AI reviewer will connect those two things across different files.


Race conditions:


These are bugs that only happen when two things occur at almost the same time. They're invisible in testing because you're one person clicking one button.


Example: your wellness engine tracks fatigue with a score that increases on each message and decays over time. Imagine a student sends two messages very quickly — maybe they hit enter twice accidentally, or their browser retries a failed request. Both requests hit the backend simultaneously. Both read the current fatigue score (say, 85%). Both calculate the new score independently (say, 91% each). Both write their result to the database. The student sent two messages but only got one fatigue increment instead of two. Now imagine the reverse — the score is at 89% and should trigger LOCKOUT at 90%, but because both requests read 89% before either writes, neither triggers the lockout.


This never shows up in testing because you send one message at a time and wait for the response. It never shows up in AI review because each function in isolation is correct. It only appears when 25 students in a classroom are all using MAIT simultaneously and the server is handling concurrent writes to the same database.


With SQLite specifically this is even worse — SQLite locks the entire database file on write. Two simultaneous writes don't create a race condition, they create a crash. One request gets a "database is locked" error and fails entirely. The student sees an error message for no apparent reason, can't reproduce it, and thinks MAIT is broken.


Edge cases under real load:


These are situations that literally cannot occur during development but are inevitable in production.


Example: a student's internet drops mid-request. The browser sent the POST to /interact, your backend received it, called Gemini, got the response, saved it to the database, but the response back to the browser failed because the student's WiFi died. From the backend's perspective, everything worked. From the student's perspective, they got an error. They refresh and send the same question again. Now you have a duplicate message in the conversation history and the fatigue score incremented twice for one question.


Example: a student pastes an entire essay into the chat box. Your system dutifully sends it to Gemini with the full system prompt, syllabus context, and conversation history. The total token count exceeds the model's context window. Gemini returns an error. But your error handling just shows "Something went wrong." The student has no idea why. They try again with the same essay. Same error. They think MAIT is broken. An AI reviewer sees your error handling and says "looks good, errors are caught." It doesn't think about what inputs a real 16-year-old would actually send.


Example: Render's free tier goes to sleep after 15 minutes. A student opens MAIT, the first request takes 40 seconds while the server cold-starts. The frontend has a 30-second timeout. The request fails. The student clicks again, this time the server is warm, it works in 2 seconds. The student now thinks MAIT is unreliable because it failed the first time. An AI reviewing your frontend timeout logic and your backend startup logic would approve both independently. The bug is in the interaction between two systems that are each individually correct.


The common thread: All of these are problems that emerge from the system — the interaction between components, users, networks, and time — rather than from any individual function being wrong. AI reviewers are excellent at evaluating functions. They're poor at simulating systems. That's the gap only you can fill, and specifically only you can fill it by watching real students actually use the thing and seeing what breaks.

Thought process: Weighed OAuth's authorization benefits against architectural nuances.

The user is asking whether using Google Sheets as their database layer, with Google OAuth, would inherently solve the security issues I raised about the student_id endpoint vulnerability. Let me think about this.

If they use Google OAuth + Google Sheets where each student's data lives in their own Google Sheet in their own Google account, then yes - the authorization problem is largely solved by Google's infrastructure. A student can only access sheets in their own Google account. The OAuth token scopes what data the app can access.

But there are nuances to think through.


Yeah, actually — this is one of the strongest arguments for the Sheets approach. It solves the authorization problem architecturally rather than in your code.


With the current SQLite setup, your backend is the gatekeeper. It stores everyone's data in one database, and your code has to enforce "Student A can only see Student A's data." If your code has a bug, everyone's data leaks. That's the vulnerability I described.


With Google Sheets via OAuth, the gatekeeper is Google. Each student authenticates with their own Google account. The OAuth token gives MAIT permission to read/write sheets in that student's Drive. Student A's token physically cannot access Student B's sheet because it lives in a completely different Google account. There's no API endpoint to exploit because the authorization boundary isn't your code — it's Google's infrastructure.


So yes, the student_id spoofing attack I described becomes impossible. You don't even have student IDs anymore. You have OAuth tokens scoped to individual Google accounts.


What it doesn't solve:


Your backend still sees the data in transit. When a student sends a message, your server receives it, processes it, calls Gemini, and writes the result to their Sheet. During that window, your server has the content in memory. This isn't a vulnerability exactly, but it means "MAIT never sees your data" wouldn't be accurate for the cloud tier. Be precise in your privacy policy.


Token expiry and refresh. OAuth access tokens expire (usually after an hour). If a student is mid-study-session and their token expires, the Sheets write fails. You need to handle token refresh silently using the refresh token, or the student gets a random error 45 minutes into studying. This is the kind of edge case AI reviewers miss.


Scope creep risk. When you request Google OAuth scopes, ask for the minimum. You need https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets.file (access only to files your app creates) — NOT https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets (access to ALL their spreadsheets). A school CEO will absolutely ask what permissions you request, and "access to all your child's Google Sheets" is a very different conversation than "access only to the MAIT data sheet."


Sheets API rate limits. Google gives you 300 requests per minute per project, 60 per minute per user. In a normal tutoring session that's fine. But if you're writing keystroke psychometrics data at high frequency, you'll hit it. Batch your writes — collect data locally and flush to the Sheet every 30 seconds rather than on every keystroke.


Offline/downtime handling. If Google's API is down (rare but it happens), your entire data layer is gone. With SQLite, at least the backend keeps working. With Sheets as the database, a Google outage means MAIT can't read conversation history, mastery scores, or anything. Have a graceful fallback — the chat should still work even if the Sheet is unreachable, just without history.


The bottom line: The Sheets approach trades "I have to build auth correctly" for "I have to handle API reliability and token management correctly." That's a good trade for a solo dev because Google's auth is battle-tested by billions of users, whereas your hand-rolled auth would be battle-tested by you. Just go in with eyes open about what the new failure modes are.

Here's the full arsenal of LaTeX/TikZ packages and features worth showcasing in your exemplar worksheet. Organised by subject area so Gemini (in a fresh chat) can generate each section.


Maths (your core)


pgfplots — the big one for function graphing. Handles 2D and 3D plots, domain control, axis labels, legends, grid lines. You give it \addplot {x^2 - 3*x + 2}; and it draws the parabola with proper axes, ticks, and labels. Supports shading areas under curves (integration visualisation), asymptotes, and multiple functions on one axis.


TikZ core — axes with arrows, tick marks, numbered gridlines, and plotted points. Good for coordinate geometry questions, vectors, and piecewise functions.


TikZ geometry libraries — calc, angles, quotes, intersections. These let you draw labelled triangles with angle arcs, perpendicular markers, parallel line notation, circle theorems with inscribed angles, and tangent lines. Essential for trig and geometry questions.


tkz-euclide — purpose-built for Euclidean geometry diagrams. Midpoints, bisectors, circumscribed circles, medians. Cleaner than raw TikZ for geometry.


Answer Space & Worksheet Formatting


Ruled lines — \rule{\linewidth}{0.4pt} for single lines, or use \foreach loops to generate sets of ruled writing lines with custom spacing. Good for "show your working" space.


Grid/graph paper — TikZ can draw grid paper with \draw[step=0.5cm, gray, very thin] for students to plot their own graphs.


Blank coordinate axes — pre-drawn axes with gridlines but no function plotted, with a question asking students to sketch the curve.


Dotted answer lines — \dotfill or custom dashed lines for fill-in-the-blank style answers.


Answer boxes — \framebox[width][alignment]{space} or TikZ rectangles for boxed final answer areas.


Working space — \vspace{4cm} for blank working areas between questions.


Chemistry (for expansion beyond maths)


mhchem — the standard for chemical formulae. \ce{H2O}, \ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}, \ce{SO4^{2-}}. Handles subscripts, superscripts, charges, arrows, and states of matter automatically.


chemfig — structural diagrams. Draws benzene rings, Lewis structures, reaction schemes with TikZ under the hood. Ring notation: \chemfig{*6(-=-=-=)} for benzene.


MOdiagram — molecular orbital diagrams for senior chemistry.


English & Humanities


Quote blocks — \begin{quote}...\end{quote} for indented passage extracts. Add \itshape for italics. Works for English comprehension passages, source analysis in history.


epigraph package — for formatted literary quotations with attribution.


Lined writing space — repeating ruled lines for essay or short answer responses, achievable with TikZ \foreach loops drawing horizontal lines at regular intervals.


Two-column layouts — multicol package for source comparison tasks (Source A vs Source B side by side).


General Visual Elements


Tables — tabular and booktabs for clean data tables in statistics questions, scientific data recording, or comparison tasks.


Boxed theorems/formulas — tcolorbox package for highlighted formula reference boxes, definition boxes, or "Key Information" callouts at the top of worksheets.


Headers/footers — fancyhdr for school name, subject, date, page numbers, and "Name: ________" fields.


Watermarks — draftwatermark for "PRACTICE" or "SAMPLE" overlays.


QR codes — qrcode package to embed a QR code linking to the MAIT answer key or tutorial video.

That's a perfect tier split. The economics are brutal in a good way:


Free tier (Gemini Canvas): Student or teacher clicks generate, prompt copies to clipboard, Gemini opens, Canvas renders the full LaTeX. Works great for one-shot worksheets. Cost to you per worksheet: fractions of a cent. Cost to the teacher per edit: seconds instead of minutes.


The token efficiency alone justifies the $5/week. Gemini regenerating 3000 tokens of LaTeX to change one question is like reprinting an entire textbook because of a typo. Your native canvas sends maybe 200 tokens for the same edit. That's a 15x efficiency gain that translates directly into speed for the teacher and cost savings for you.

MAIT Native Canvas — Feature Overview
The Native Canvas is a block-based LaTeX worksheet editor embedded in MyAITutor's Worksheet Studio. It replaces the old monolithic "generate then download" flow with an interactive, fragment-level editing experience powered by AI.
Architecture
Split-pane editor: left pane is a sortable list of LaTeX fragments; right pane is a live PDF preview compiled via pdflatex.
Data flow: User configures worksheet (year level, subject, topics, difficulty) → Gemini generates a LaTeX enumerate block → backend decomposes it into individually editable elements → frontend renders them in a Zustand-powered store → user edits, reorders, compiles, and exports.
Data Model (SQLite)
Table Purpose documents Worksheet metadata (title, student, source, year/subject) document_elements Individual LaTeX fragments with LexoRank sort keys document_revisions AI revision history (input/output snapshots, status) artifact_builds Compilation records (status, PDF path, error logs)
Element Types & Structure
Each worksheet decomposes into typed elements with semantic sort keys:
Kind Sort Key Locked Purpose preamble a0 Yes \documentclass, packages, page geometry header a1 No Title, Name/Date fields text_block (List Start) a2_a_start Yes \begin{enumerate} question (×N) a2_b_000…a2_b_NNN No Individual \item entries text_block (List End) a2_c_end Yes \end{enumerate} text_block (Watermark) a2_d_wm No myaitutor.au/worksheets footer mark footer a3 Yes \end{document}
Locked elements prevent accidental structural damage. Collapsed by default to reduce clutter.
Backend Services
artifact_engine.py — Gemini-powered LaTeX generation + pdflatex compilation


Generates NESA-style maths questions with TikZ diagrams

Compiles with --no-shell-escape security flag

Runs pdflatex twice (for page references)

Package allowlist: amsmath, amssymb, geometry, tikz, tcolorbox, fancyhdr, enumitem, etc.
latex_decomposer.py — Splits Gemini's monolithic output into fragments

Depth-aware regex parser that tracks \begin{}/\end{} nesting

Only splits on top-level \item entries, preserving sub-environments
revision_service.py — AI element revision

Sends a single fragment + instruction to Gemini Flash

Stores before/after snapshots for preview → apply/reject workflow
image_to_fragment_service.py — Vision parsing

Sends uploaded image to Gemini Flash Vision

Returns structured JSON array of fragments

Smart placeholder bail-out: complex diagrams get a dashed tcolorbox placeholder instead of broken TikZ
element_service.py — CRUD for elements with sort key management
API Endpoints (13 total)
Method Route Purpose POST /canvas/generate Generate worksheet from config GET /canvas/documents List student's worksheets GET /canvas/documents/{id} Get document + elements DELETE /canvas/documents/{id} Delete worksheet POST /canvas/documents/{id}/elements Add element PUT /canvas/elements/{id} Update element DELETE /canvas/elements/{id} Delete element POST /canvas/compile Compile LaTeX → base64 PDF POST /canvas/elements/{id}/revise Request AI revision POST /canvas/revisions/{id}/apply Apply revision POST /canvas/revisions/{id}/reject Reject revision GET /canvas/documents/{id}/revisions List revision history POST /canvas/documents/{id}/vision-parse Image → LaTeX fragments
Frontend Components
InlineCanvas — Root container. Two-pane layout, keyboard shortcuts (Ctrl+Shift+P to compile, Ctrl+S to save), .tex/.pdf export, fallback to local scaffold if backend is unreachable.
ElementList — Sortable vertical list with @dnd-kit drag-and-drop. Each card shows kind badge (color-coded), label, content preview. Expanded view reveals Monaco LaTeX editor, AI revise button, move/duplicate/delete actions.
PdfPreviewPane — Right pane with iframe PDF viewer, zoom controls (50–200%), download button, compilation spinner.
RevisionPanel — Overlay for AI editing. Type an instruction or use quick buttons ("Make harder", "Add hint", "Simplify", "Add part (b)", "Change numbers"). Shows before/after diff preview with apply/reject.
ScanQuestionModal — Drag-and-drop image upload. Sends photo of handwritten/printed questions to Gemini Vision, returns parsed LaTeX fragments ready to insert.
InsertElementMenu — Template library organized by category (Questions, Diagrams, Instructions, Worked Examples, Headers). Also offers "From Image" to trigger vision scanning.
CompileErrorBanner — Sticky error bar with human-friendly message + expandable raw pdflatex log.
Key Design Decisions


Fractional indexing (LexoRank) for sort keys — enables drag-and-drop reordering without reindexing all elements

Optimistic updates with 1500ms debounced persistence — responsive editing without excessive API calls

Locked structural elements — preamble, enumerate wrappers, and footer are non-editable to prevent compilation breakage

Modular compilation — elements are concatenated into a single .tex file at compile time; each fragment is independently editable

Vision parse bail-out — Gemini outputs placeholder boxes for diagrams it can't faithfully reproduce, rather than generating broken TikZ

This is really well-crafted. A few issues to flag:


The Whiteout Rule will cause problems on coloured backgrounds. If a teacher ever uses a coloured tcolorbox or shaded region, fill=white nodes will create visible white rectangles. Consider fill=white, fill opacity=0.85 as a softer alternative, or note in the prompt that this assumes white page background.


\dfrac everywhere is aggressive. It's correct for standalone display equations but inside inline text it'll blow out line spacing. Change the rule to: "Use \dfrac{}{} for display math and \frac{}{} for inline math."


\needspace{6cm} before every \item is a lot. Short one-line questions don't need 6cm of guaranteed space. That'll create unnecessary page breaks on compact worksheets. Consider \needspace{3cm} as default, with \needspace{6cm} only before questions that contain TikZ diagrams or tcolorboxes.


Missing pgfplots from the preamble. Your exemplar worksheet had function graphs and coordinate planes. If Gemini tries to use \begin{axis}...\end{axis} for graphing, it'll fail without \usepackage{pgfplots} and \pgfplotsset{compat=1.18}. Add both to the preamble.


Missing mhchem for chemistry. Your exemplar had the aspirin structural formula. If a teacher selects Chemistry as the subject, Gemini will need \usepackage[version=4]{mhchem} and \usepackage{chemfig}. Either add them to the default preamble (they're lightweight and won't conflict) or add a conditional note: "If the subject is Chemistry, add mhchem and chemfig to the preamble."


The greeting will get repetitive fast. A teacher iterating 15 times on a worksheet sees "Here's your updated worksheet! Let me know if you want to tweak..." every single time. Consider shortening the follow-up greeting to just the code block after the 3rd interaction, or adding: "After the third exchange, skip the greeting and output only the LaTeX code block."


No explicit instruction about mark allocations. Your UI shows [2M], [3M] badges on questions. Add a rule: "Each question MUST end with a mark allocation in square brackets, e.g. [2 Marks]. Distribute marks based on complexity — 1-2 for recall, 3-4 for application, 5+ for multi-step analysis."


The multicol answer key can break with TikZ. If the answer key includes diagrams or worked solutions with displayed equations, two-column layout will overflow. Add: "If an answer requires a diagram or more than 4 lines of working, break out of multicols for that answer using \end{multicols} ... answer ... \begin{multicols}{2}."


One structural concern: You say "Print exactly ONE single LaTeX code block" but what happens when the teacher asks a clarifying question like "what topics can you cover?" The model is forced to output LaTeX even when the conversation doesn't warrant it. Add an exception: "If the user's message is a question or request for information rather than a worksheet modification, respond conversationally WITHOUT a LaTeX code block."


Otherwise this is tight. The TikZ quality controls especially — the angle library enforcement and the ban on absolute label positioning will prevent 90% of the broken diagram issues that plague AI-generated LaTeX.

Here's what TurboQuant is and why you should care as a MAIT builder:


The short version: Google Research dropped a compression algorithm on 25/03/26 that shrinks an LLM's working memory (the KV cache) by ~6x with near-zero accuracy loss at 3-3.5 bits per value, and no retraining required. Cloudflare's CEO called it "Google's DeepSeek moment." The internet is calling it the real-world Pied Piper from Silicon Valley.


What the KV cache actually is: When a model generates tokens, it stores all prior token context in memory so it doesn't have to recompute everything for each new token. As prompts and outputs get longer, this memory grows quickly. At long context lengths (128k+ tokens), the KV cache takes up more GPU memory than the model weights themselves.


The numbers: TurboQuant compresses the KV cache to 3.5 bits per value with near-zero accuracy loss on benchmarks like LongBench and Needle in a Haystack, matching 16-bit precision performance across Gemma and Mistral models. 4-bit TurboQuant achieves up to 8x performance increase over 32-bit unquantized keys on H100 GPUs.


How it works in plain English: Two stages. First, it rotates data vectors using a randomized Hadamard transform, which spreads out values and removes the outlier-heavy distribution that makes low-bit quantization difficult. Second, a decade-old trick (Quantized Johnson-Lindenstrauss) corrects the bias introduced by the first step. One bit of compression power goes to the error-checking stage, the rest goes to the actual compression.


Why it matters for MAIT specifically:


Your long tutoring sessions generate substantial conversation history. When Gemini is processing a student's 20th message in a session with full syllabus context + chat history + keystroke metadata + Bloom's state, the KV cache for that request is the dominant memory cost on Google's side. At 128k context in FP16, a request can need 40GB just for KV cache; TurboQuant would reduce that to 7.5GB.


This doesn't change anything you can touch as a developer — you don't control Google's inference infrastructure. But it does change the economics of what Google can offer you. Either Flash-Lite gets cheaper at scale, or the context windows get bigger at the same price, or both. Your BYOK free tier becomes more sustainable for Google to support.


For your WebLLM free demo: There's already a working TurboQuant implementation in llama.cpp with 18/18 tests passing, plus PyTorch implementations from the community. Once WebLLM adopts it (likely in the coming months), your Gemma 4 E2B demo model that currently needs ~200MB could theoretically run at similar quality with significantly less memory. Better mobile experience, faster load times.


The hardware market reaction is the interesting part: Micron and SanDisk both sold off at market open after TurboQuant was announced, because if inference needs 6x less memory, the projected demand for high-bandwidth memory just got cut. This is exactly the pattern you've been predicting — efficiency gains compressing the AI infrastructure market. China's DeepSeek did it with training, Google's doing it with inference.


Your philosophical angle: TurboQuant + Gemma 4 + Flash-Lite pricing is the same trajectory — AI keeps getting dramatically cheaper to serve at frontier quality. Your MAIT unit economics were already absurd at 99% margins. This trajectory makes them more so. The "wait, why isn't everyone building specialised AI products right now" moment keeps getting louder.

what can i use agent swarms for?

Agent swarms are parallelised AI execution — multiple agents working on different parts of a task simultaneously rather than sequentially. Think of it as "multiprocessing for AI tasks" instead of waiting for one long prompt to complete.


Where swarms genuinely help you on MAIT:


1. Parallel codebase audits. Spawn 5 agents, each looking at a different slice — frontend state management, backend security, LaTeX prompt quality, database schema, deployment config. Each produces a focused report. You get a full audit in the time a single-agent audit would take to just scan the frontend.


2. Test generation at scale. You have zero automated tests. Swarm 10 agents, each writing tests for a different module — canvas store, API client, keystroke service, PII filter, Bloom's engine, etc. Hours of parallel work producing a test suite you'd otherwise never write.


3. Multi-subject syllabus expansion. When you expand from Maths Advanced to Extension 1, Extension 2, Chemistry, Physics — each subject needs its own syllabus JSON, prompt templates, pedagogical drills, example worksheets. Swarm one agent per subject. They research NESA content in parallel, produce structured output, you review.


4. Question bank generation. Swarm agents to generate thousands of practice questions per topic, each agent specialising in a topic area. They produce questions, answer keys, difficulty ratings. You get a 10,000-question bank in the time one agent would generate 500.


5. Documentation sweeps. Every file in your codebase needing docstrings, every API endpoint needing OpenAPI docs, every component needing a README — swarm it. One-shot, massive parallel coverage.


6. Translation for accessibility. You mentioned ESL support earlier. Swarm agents to translate your UI strings into 10+ languages simultaneously. Faster than any translation service.


7. Screenshot and demo content generation. Need marketing screenshots of every feature for your Substack, LinkedIn, the pitch deck, the CEO handout? Swarm agents to navigate the site, capture screenshots at specific viewports, generate alt text. Much faster than you manually clicking through.


Where swarms are overkill or counterproductive:


Architectural decisions — you want one strong model thinking carefully, not five parallel opinions. Architecture needs coherence, which swarms fight against.


Sequential dependencies — if Task B needs Task A's output, you can't parallelise. Most coding is like this.


Prompt-sensitive work — your worksheet LaTeX generation is finely tuned. A swarm would produce inconsistent output because each agent interprets the prompt slightly differently.


Debugging — you want deep context, not breadth. Swarms dilute attention.


My specific recommendation for MAIT right now:


Save the swarm ammunition for the subject expansion phase. Once you've nailed Maths Advanced with the CEO pilot, expanding to Extension 1, Extension 2, Chemistry, Physics, Biology, English in parallel is a legitimate multi-week swarm project. Each subject agent produces: syllabus JSON, 500+ practice questions, pedagogy templates, example worksheets, answer keys. You review and integrate.


For immediate work, keep using single agents. Your current bottleneck is coherent architectural decisions (auth, database, Canvas frontend), not throughput of parallel tasks.

Two codebases means two deployment pipelines, two bug surfaces, two versions of every feature. Feature parity between web and mobile is a maintenance tax forever.

App Store and Play Store review cycles are slower than your build velocity. A bug you ship at 2am can't be hotfixed until Apple approves it 24-72 hours later.

Three realistic paths, in order of how I'd rank them for your situation:


Option A: React Native + on-device inference (Recommended)

Expo for easy development, eject when you need native modules for inference

Option B: Flutter + on-device inference

On the Skinner Box question:


You're right to be suspicious of yourself — the bookshelf logbook flick is genuinely on the line. The cleanest test is: does the feedback shift the student's locus of evaluation from internal to external?


A real-world equivalent: a piano teacher who says "you nailed that arpeggio" is fine. A piano teacher who pulls out a logbook every time you play to show you a chart of your improvement is making the chart the point.


The fix isn't to remove acknowledgement — humans need to feel seen. The fix is to make the acknowledgement informational rather than evaluative. State of the Platform — Late April 2026


MAIT is a working production system at myaitutor.au with 137+ commits, organic teacher adoption, and a credible technical architecture. The core value proposition — privacy-first AI tutoring with pedagogical safety guardrails — is technically real, not vapourware. The product is closer to launch than most solo-built platforms achieve, and further from launch than the strategic conversations would suggest.


Architecture


The system runs a Bring Your Own Key model where free tier users supply their own Gemini API keys, eliminating per-user inference cost to MAIT. The Dual-Agent Routing Architecture — Generator drafts response, Evaluator validates against pedagogical and mathematical guardrails, Router applies up to two revision loops before falling back to a safe Socratic default — is specced and ready for implementation but not yet shipped. The Native Canvas IDE for teachers is the most architecturally mature component: 13 REST endpoints, Monaco editor for fragment-level LaTeX editing, LexoRank fractional indexing for drag-and-drop reordering, integrated AI revision and vision parsing, full PDF compilation pipeline. Backend is fully wired to live Gemini generation. Frontend is currently mounting hardcoded dummy fragments and needs Codex to complete the wiring — prompt written, awaiting execution.


WebLLM browser-only demo mode runs SmolLM2 1.7B, Llama 3.2 3B, and Phi 3.5 Mini behind a consent gate that respects bandwidth and storage. Gemma 4 swap is blocked on WebLLM's model registry adding support — likely weeks away. The three-tier student safety protocol (graduated escalation through reflective acknowledgement, peer-support resource bridging like ReachOut, and crisis-line redirection) is designed but not implemented in code.


Economics


Per-session inference cost on Gemini Flash-Lite sits at approximately $0.02. The Dual-Agent verification circuit adds roughly $0.0007 per response on average. At proposed pricing of $5/week for the teacher tier and $10-15/week for student tier, gross margins are approximately 99% on compute. Break-even on the teacher tier sits at about 1,785 worksheets per week per teacher, which is two orders of magnitude beyond realistic usage. The economics are not the constraint. The constraint is everything else.


Outstanding Critical Issues


Three blockers from the Gemini architectural audit remain open. SQLite running on Render's ephemeral filesystem means student data evaporates on every server spin-down — Codex completed the migration to Neon Postgres on a feature branch yesterday, smoke test pending, merge blocked on that smoke test. The IDOR vulnerability where the X-Student-Id header is string-matched without cryptographic validation means any student can spoof another student's identity to access or modify their data. JWT migration is specced, blocked on Postgres completion (now unblocked), execution pending. The keystroke biometric parental consent flow under Australian Privacy Principles is the third critical — the legal framing has been corrected ("Engagement Telemetry" rather than "psychometric profiling") but the actual consent UI has not been built.


Adoption Signal


Native Canvas has organic teacher pickup — staff at Darra's placement school have been shown the worksheet generator, parents and students have seen demos and reacted positively, the assessor on his demonstration lesson saw it briefly and engaged. Forward Plan — Next 60-90 Days


What Ships in 30 Days


The CEO meeting is the dominant constraint. Three things must close before that conversation can credibly support a B2B licensing pitch.


The Postgres migration must merge to production. The IDOR vulnerability must be replaced with proper JWT auth bound to Google OAuth. The privacy policy and parental consent flow for Engagement Telemetry must be live on the site. These three are not negotiable — without them, the pitch is "trust me, the architecture is sound" which fails any technical due diligence the school's IT director will conduct after the meeting.


Of those three, the parental consent flow blocks the B2B licensing conversation most directly. A school cannot legally onboard students to a behavioural data-collecting platform without parental consent, and explaining how that's handled is the first question a CEO will ask. SQLite-on-ephemeral-filesystem and IDOR are technical embarrassments that won't surface in the meeting itself but will surface in due diligence within two weeks of the meeting. Ship it independently of the CEO meeting outcome. The article is currently positioned as a build-in-public document, and the credibility play works whether the first CEO meeting succeeds or not. Holding it back to coordinate with a successful pilot announcement is over-engineering — most readers will never connect the two events temporally, and the article's value compounds the longer it's been live and indexed. Publish in the next two weeks. Update later with pilot announcements as separate posts.

Realistic B2B Pilot Timeline


The earliest the first school pilot can legitimately begin is six weeks from now, assuming the three critical blockers close in the 30-day window and the pilot proposal is signed in week 5-6. That puts pilot start at early June 2026, with first useful usage data in late June and substantive feedback by end of July. This is the optimistic case.


Realistic case is pilot start in early Term 3 — late July or early August — once school administrative cycles align and any initial pushback from teaching staff or parents has been addressed. That's three months from now.


The constraint is not technical. The constraint is institutional. Schools move slowly even when motivated. The CEO meeting succeeding does not equal the pilot starting two weeks later.


What the RSI Context Changes


The frontier capability discontinuity emerging now creates a strategic pull in two directions, and the right answer is not "ship faster."


The case for ship faster: capability is increasing exponentially, every month MAIT delays is a month where Gemini and Claude alone become more credible substitutes for the wellness-first pedagogical layer MAIT provides. Speed wins.


The case for patient credibility: in a landscape where every major player is shipping AI products at a pace that erodes user trust faster than they can rebuild it, the slow, deliberate, safety-first product wins by being the option schools actually trust to put in front of minors. The market is starting to differentiate between "AI-native" and "AI-careful." MAIT's positioning is the latter.


Resolution: the right move is patient credibility-building, but only because the technical foundation is already mostly there. If MAIT were two months from a working MVP, ship faster would dominate. Because MAIT is two weeks from production-ready (modulo the three blockers), the marginal value of additional speed is low and the marginal value of additional rigour is high. Close the three blockers properly. Run the pilot with real safety infrastructure in place. Publish the build story to establish public positioning. Use the next 90 days to compound credibility.


The RSI context changes one specific calculation: any feature that depends on frontier model capability rather than careful product design becomes less defensible over time. Don't build features that GPT-5.5 or Claude Opus 4.7 would render obsolete in six months. Build features that depend on integration with NSW curriculum, Australian privacy law, school-specific deployment, teacher workflow understanding — the moats that capability discontinuity does not erode.


The One Genuine Uncertainty


The single point of real uncertainty is whether the CEO meeting actually converts. Deputy Principal Zamil's enthusiasm is genuine but does not guarantee CEO buy-in. The CEO of an independent school manages a complex set of stakeholders — the board, the parents, the teaching union, the IT department, the legal team — and a 21-year-old SLSO walking in with an impressive AI demo is not automatically welcomed regardless of how good the demo is. The pitch needs to address all five of those audiences in advance.


If the meeting succeeds, the 90-day plan above is roughly correct. If it doesn't, the plan needs to pivot harder toward independent school outreach, content marketing, and parent-direct B2C — a slower path but not a fatal one. Don't bet everything on this single meeting. The pilot pipeline needs at least three school conversations in flight by the time the CEO meeting happens, so a failed conversion isn't a stopped pipeline.


That's the real strategic open question. Not "will MAIT work" — it works. Not "is the market there" — the market is there. The question is whether the first institutional door opens cleanly or has to be pried open through several attempts.

The git terminology you might be missing:


When you "merge a feature branch into main," you're saying "take all the changes from this feature and add them to the main timeline." After merging, the feature branch can be deleted (the changes live on in main).


When you "branch FROM main," you're creating a new timeline that starts where main currently is. If main has been updated since the feature branch was made, the feature branch doesn't automatically know about those updates.


Three feature branches all created from the same old main version means each one is missing the others' changes. Merging them in sequence puts them back together on the main timeline.
